# Churn Analysis

### Loading Packages & Connecting to the Database

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
# for database connection
library(RPostgres)
library(DBI)
# for survival analysis
library(survival)
library(survminer)

# edit these
DB_NAME <- 'subscription_churn'
DB_USER <- 'postgres'
DB_PASS <- 'postgres'
DB_HOST <- 'localhost'
DB_PORT <- '5432'

con <- dbConnect(Postgres(),
                 host = DB_HOST,
                 port = DB_PORT,
                 dbname = DB_NAME,
                 user = DB_USER,
                 password = DB_PASS)

dbListTables(con)
```

### Loading Data

Joining the members and events tables, using data in or after 2015. Low-frequency cities and registration methods are grouped under OTHER. The three most popular tiers, namely NT\\\\\$99, NT\\\\\$129, and NT\\\\\$149, are chosen to compare.

```{r}
df <-dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT 
      events.member_id,
      city, 
      registration_method, 
      is_complete_age_gender, 
      tenure_id, 
      avg_price, 
      start_day, 
      end_day,
      event
  FROM events
  INNER JOIN members
  ON events.member_id = members.member_id
  WHERE avg_price IN (99, 129, 149)
    AND registration_date >= '2015-01-01 00:00:00';
"
) %>%
  add_count(city, name = 'city_count') %>%
  add_count(registration_method, name = 'regis_count') %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    city = if_else(city_count/n() < 0.05,
                   "OTHER",
                   city),
    registration_method = if_else(regis_count/n() < 0.05,
                                  "OTHER",
                                  registration_method),
    pricing_tier = as.character(avg_price)
  ) %>%
  select(-city_count, -regis_count)
head(df)
```

### Kaplan-Meier Curves

```{r}
surv_obj <- Surv(time = df$start_day,
                 time2 = df$end_day, 
                 event = df$event)

km_fit <- surv_fit(surv_obj ~ 1, data = df)

ggsurvplot(km_fit,
           conf.int = TRUE,
           risk.table = TRUE,
           linewidth = 0.1,
           censor.size = 0,
           break.time.by = 360,
           surv.plot.height = 1,
           risk.table.height = 0.3,
           risk.table.fontsize = 2,
           xlab = 'Subscription Tenure (Days)',
           ylab = 'Retention Rate',
           ggtheme = theme_minimal())
```

Stratifying by pricing tier. It is shown that the higher the price, the lower the associated retention rate.

```{r}
km_price <- surv_fit(surv_obj ~ 1 + pricing_tier, data = df)

names(km_price$strata) <- gsub("pricing_tier=", "", names(km_price$strata))

ggsurvplot(km_price,
           conf.int = TRUE,
           risk.table = TRUE,
           linewidth = 0.1,
           censor.size = 0,
           break.time.by = 360,
           surv.plot.height = 1,
           risk.table.height = 0.4,
           risk.table.fontsize = 2,
           legend.title = 'Pricing Tier',
           xlab = 'Subscription Tenure (Days)',
           ylab = 'Retention Rate',
           ggtheme = theme_minimal())
```

Stratifying by city. City 1 is associated with a higher retention rate than the other cities, whereas the retention rates of the other cities are similar to each other.

```{r}

km_city <- surv_fit(surv_obj ~ 1 + city, data = df)

names(km_city$strata) <- gsub("city=", "", names(km_city$strata))

ggsurvplot(km_city,
           conf.int = TRUE,
           risk.table = TRUE,
           linewidth = 0.1,
           censor.size = 0,
           break.time.by = 360,
           surv.plot.height = 1,
           risk.table.height = 0.5,
           risk.table.fontsize = 2,
           legend.title = 'City',
           xlab = 'Subscription Tenure (Days)',
           ylab = 'Retention Rate',
           ggtheme = theme_minimal())
```

### The Model

A Cox Proportional Hazards Model is used, with the price and city as covariates. An interaction between them is also introduced.

$$ h(t) = h_0(t)\cdot\exp\bigl[\beta_1\cdot\text{pricing\_tier} + \beta_2\cdot\text{city} + \beta_3\cdot(\text{pricing\_tier}\cdot\text{city})\bigr] $$

Plotting the Schoenfeld residuals against time, it can be seen that all the residuals stay relatively constant up till 365 days. That means that there is no evidence against the proportional hazards assumption for short term predictions.

```{r}
cox_fit <- coxph(surv_obj ~ pricing_tier*city, data = df)
plot(cox.zph(cox_fit))
```

### Results

The pricing tier effects are significant but not the city effects, except for the marginally significant effect of city 13. Looking at the interaction effects, the only significant one is the 149 tier in city 13. The churn risk associated with the 149 tier is 1.6665 times that of the 129 tier, and the risk associated with the 99 tier is 0.2061 times that of the 129 tier. The churn risk of 149 has 0.7807 times the effect on city 13 compared to city 1.

```{r}
summary(cox_fit)
```

Predicting the median survival times of each tier in city 1. It is not worth increasing the price to 149 as the churn risk outweighs the extra revenue.

```{r}
survfit(
  cox_fit, 
  newdata = data.frame(
    pricing_tier = c('99', '129', '149'), 
    city = '1')
)
```

Even in city 13, the churn risk just barely surpasses the extra revenue.

```{r}
survfit(
  cox_fit, 
  newdata = data.frame(
    pricing_tier = c('99', '129', '149'), 
    city = '13')
)
```
